country.comment: Study investigates the rural community of Nanka in Anambra State, southeastern Nigeria.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Abstract; PDF p. 6, Section 3 (Materials and Methods)

effect_estimate.comment: Qualitative study reporting descriptive response percentages from 105 household interviews alongside thematic findings from interviews, bylaw review, and field observation; no inferential statistical effect estimates are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported (descriptive interview frequencies only: communal bylaws prohibit boreholes/wells and certain streams while mandating floodwater ditches enforced via fines and community service, and zero state-allocated town union funds were channeled to water projects; households rely on rainwater harvesting [86%; 0% drink ditch water, 11% (n = 12) drink boiled tank rainwater], public streams/rivers [73% source; 48% fetching as coping strategy], and commercial tankers/sachet water vendors [57% source; 26% (n = 27) buy year-round; ~50% rely on sachet water for drinking year-round], alongside water sharing [64%]; 98% [n = 103] report awareness of water sourcing problems, but 75% [n = 79] do not view them as severe enough to attract external intervention).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Design ceiling for a qualitative study appraised with CASP is 2. The study directly observes and documents communal bylaws, committee inspections, monetary/community-service sanctions, and town union fund-allocation practices shaping domestic water access through document analysis of community bylaws, field observation, and interviews with 25 community leaders, 3 government officials, and 105 households.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines communal bylaws prohibiting borehole/well drilling on land, forbidding access to sacred streams, and mandating premise drainage ditches ('mgbacha ogwugwu') (ELIGIBILITY / property); strict local inspection and monetary fines or community service for non-compliance or missing mandatory male-only annual assemblies (ENFORCEMENT / sanction); and community assembly participation, discretionary non-allocation of state development grants by the town union to water projects, and multi-tier state/local/community/NGO coordination gaps (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION / participation, discretion, political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, property, discretion, sanction, participation, political_coordination

outcome_flags.comment: Directly examines household domestic and drinking water access across sources, dry-season storage tank capacity and water exhaustion (service_quantity), potability/contamination and household alum/boiling treatment (service_quality), and financial burden of concrete tanks and vended/sachet water purchases (affordability). No piped utility network exists in the community.

publication_year.comment: Published 12 August 2022 in Resources (2022, Volume 11, Article 77).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, citation header, publication history, and copyright notice

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Authors explicitly adopt a qualitative research design (in-depth semi-structured interviews, document analysis of literature and community bylaws, and exploratory field observation analyzed via grounded theory and axial coding) and explicitly reject quantitative survey/experimental methods in Section 4; descriptive percentages summarize interview responses rather than constituting a separate quantitative analytical component.

sample_size.comment: From a clan-recorded population frame of 4,336 households (calculated minimum sample of 98 households at 10% precision), 14 households per village across 7 villages were purposively selected (105 household heads: 81 women and 24 men), supplemented by purposive interviews with 25 community leaders, 7 leaders of thought, and 3 government officials (total N = 140 formal interview respondents), plus informal reconnaissance interviews, document analysis, and field observation.
sample_size.value: 140 interview respondents (105 household heads across 7 villages, 25 community leaders, 7 leaders of thought, and 3 government officials)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 8, Section 5; PDF p. 9, Table 2

study_design.comment: Authors frame the work as qualitative research combining semi-structured interviews (open- and closed-ended questions), document analysis (including community bylaws), and exploratory field observation, coded via grounded analysis and axial coding, with descriptive percentages reported for household interview items.
study_design.value: Qualitative case study (purposive semi-structured in-depth interviews, document/bylaw analysis, and exploratory field observation analyzed with grounded analysis and axial coding)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 7–9, Sections 4–5 and Tables 2–3

evidence_quotes.quote: These factors were investigated through qualitative research methods.
A total of 105 household heads, which included 81 women and 24 men, agreed and participated in the interview sections, which lasted for an average time of 1 h from September 2018 to January 2019.

The major identiﬁed sources are rainwater harvesting (86%) (roof water connected to tank/ﬂood water channeled to ditches), surface water—public streams and rivers (73%), and water vendors (57%) (water tankers and private factory-packaged sachet water sources from boreholes at the urban areas).
Due to the high susceptibility of these areas to erosion and landslide, there is an existing communal law that forbids the construction of boreholes or wells.

During this period, committees are appointed to inspect the entire community and supervise the adherence to the erosion and water laws, implement sanctions, and report back to the community general assembly.

“All the funds received by Nanka town union within this period, none has been channeled to community water projects. It rightly shows that water challenges are not among the collective priority need of the community.”
